library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)

# Source and models

* Citation: Johnson M, Lin YW, Schmidt H, Sunnaker M, Van Maanen E, Huang X,
  Rukazenkov Y, Tomkinson H, Vishwanathan K. Exposure-response modelling of
  osimertinib in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Br J Clin
  Pharmacol. 2024;90(12):3263-3276. doi:10.1111/bcp.16199
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16199>
* PMC open-access copy: <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11602960/>
* Supplementary Appendix (logistic-regression model form, Tables S1-S11)
  published with the open-access article. A correction notice of 30 August
  2024 updated reference 12 only and changes no model value.

Johnson 2024 relates the steady-state exposure (AUCss) of osimertinib, and of
its active metabolite AZ5104, to efficacy and safety endpoints across the
first-line, second-or-later-line and adjuvant osimertinib programme. The
safety endpoints with a fitted model are interstitial lung disease (ILD) and
left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) decrease events, each modelled by a
penalized (Firth) logistic regression. Osimertinib and AZ5104 exposures are
highly correlated (Figure S1), so each endpoint was fitted twice -- once on
each exposure -- and never with both. That gives four independent models:

| Model | Endpoint | Exposure | Covariates | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Johnson_2024_osimertinib_ild_osimertinib` | `prob_ild` | `log(AUC_OSIMERTINIB)` | `RACE_JAPANESE`, `RACE_ASIAN` | Table 1, Model 3 |
| `Johnson_2024_osimertinib_ild_az5104` | `prob_ild` | `log(AUC_AZ5104)` | `RACE_JAPANESE`, `RACE_ASIAN` | Table S7, Model 3 |
| `Johnson_2024_osimertinib_lvef_osimertinib` | `prob_lvef_decrease` | `log(AUC_OSIMERTINIB)` | `LVEF_BL` | Table 2, final model |
| `Johnson_2024_osimertinib_lvef_az5104` | `prob_lvef_decrease` | `log(AUC_AZ5104)` | `LVEF_BL` | Table 2, final model |

The models carry no PK layer: exposure is an input column. Johnson 2024 derived
it as AUCss = dose / (CL/F)_i from the individual apparent clearances of the
programme's population PK model, published as Johnson 2025 and packaged as
`Johnson_2025_osimertinib`. This vignette uses that model to build the
exposure of a virtual cohort.

```{r models}
mod_ild_osi  <- readModelDb("Johnson_2024_osimertinib_ild_osimertinib")
mod_ild_az   <- readModelDb("Johnson_2024_osimertinib_ild_az5104")
mod_lvef_osi <- readModelDb("Johnson_2024_osimertinib_lvef_osimertinib")
mod_lvef_az  <- readModelDb("Johnson_2024_osimertinib_lvef_az5104")
mod_pk       <- readModelDb("Johnson_2025_osimertinib")

mw_osimertinib <- 499.62 # g/mol, C28H33N7O2 (as in Johnson_2025_osimertinib)
fm_az5104      <- 0.25   # fixed parent-to-AZ5104 fraction of the PK model
```

What is not packaged, and why:

* **Efficacy (PFS / DFS).** Johnson 2024 analysed efficacy with Kaplan-Meier
  curves by AUCss quartile and Cox proportional-hazards regressions (Figure 1,
  Table S5). A Cox model leaves the baseline hazard unestimated, so it cannot
  be simulated, and the paper concludes there is no exposure-efficacy
  relationship in any line of therapy. The Burr baseline hazard mentioned in
  the Figure S3 caption is not reported.
* **Rash and diarrhoea.** Analysed descriptively only (Figure 4); the
  exposure-response model for these endpoints is the earlier
  `Brown_2017_osimertinib` analysis (reference 18).

# Population

The ILD and LVEF models were fitted to osimertinib-treated patients in the
first-line (AURA, FLAURA; N = 338) and second-or-later-line (AURA, AURA
extension, AURA2, AURA3; N = 1026) settings with a computable AUCss (Johnson
2024 Methods, Table S1). Across these 1364 patients (Table S3) the median age
was about 62 years (range 25-91), the median weight 60-62 kg (29-122 kg), 65%
were female, and 62% were Asian: by grouped race 18.6% Japanese, 20.3%
Chinese, 23.7% other Asian, 27.5% White and 9.9% other. Doses were 20-240 mg
once daily in AURA and 80 mg once daily elsewhere. The safety analyses used
the FIRST dose a patient received to compute AUCss. Comparator EGFR-TKI,
chemotherapy and placebo patients appear in the paper's figures for comparison
only and were not part of any fit. The adjuvant ADAURA study (N = 325) was
used to check the ILD and LVEF predictions externally.

The LVEF analysis covered 936 patients: 4 at 40 mg, 909 at 80 mg, 21 at 160 mg
and 2 at 240 mg, with 0, 35, 1 and 0 events (Results). The ILD analysis had 51
events across the AUCss quartiles of Figure 2A.

# Source trace

| Element | Value | Source location |
|---|---|---|
| Logistic model form `log(p/(1-p)) = alpha + beta_0 * C_i + covariate terms` | -- | Supplementary Methods, 'Logistic regression for ILD/LVEF' |
| Exposure `C_i` = natural log of AUCss in nM*h | -- | Results ('log-transformed ... AUCss'); Figures 2 and 3 axes; checked below |
| ILD, osimertinib: intercept / exposure / Japanese / Asian non-Japanese | -9.35 / 0.628 / 1.14 / -0.567 | Table 1, Model 3 |
| ILD, AZ5104: intercept / exposure / Japanese / Asian non-Japanese | -7.46 / 0.559 / 1.17 / -0.551 | Table S7, Model 3 |
| LVEF, osimertinib: intercept / slope / baseline LVEF | -6.36 / 0.921 / -0.087 | Table 2 (and Table S10) |
| LVEF, AZ5104: intercept / slope / baseline LVEF | -4.38 / 0.927 / -0.087 | Table 2 (and Table S11) |
| AUCss = dose / (CL/F)_i, first dose received | -- | Methods, 'Estimation of plasma exposure' |
| Population PK model for CL/F | `Johnson_2025_osimertinib` | Reference 23; NONMEM code in the Supplementary Methods |
| Placebo extrapolation 0.009% (osimertinib) and 0.06% (AZ5104) | -- | Results, 'Model simulations' |
| Event counts by dose for LVEF | 0/4, 35/909, 1/21, 0/2 | Results, 'Model-based exposure and LVEF analysis' |
| Placeholder residual `addSd_prob_*` | 0.001, fixed | Not from source (Bernoulli likelihood) |

# Check 1 -- the exposure enters as a natural log of AUCss in nM*h

Johnson 2024 states that the LVEF models used "log-transformed" AUCss but does
not say so for ILD, and neither table gives the exposure unit. The ILD model
settles both: evaluated on the natural log of AUCss in nM*h, the Table 1
Model 3 estimates reproduce the three predicted-mean curves of Figure 2C at
the quartile boundaries printed on its axis. On a linear scale, or with AUCss
in ng*h/mL or ug*h/mL, the curves would be several-fold off.

```{r check-figure-2c}
solve_er <- function(model, output, data) {
  ev <- data |> dplyr::mutate(id = dplyr::row_number(), time = 0, amt = 0, evid = 0L)
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(model, events = ev, returnType = "data.frame"))[[output]]
}

auc_axis <- c(6584.57, 9689.56, 12910.9, 21683.3) # Figure 2C x-axis ticks, nM*h

# Predicted-mean lines read off Figure 2C at the first and last tick.
fig2c <- tibble::tribble(
  ~race_group,            ~AUC_OSIMERTINIB, ~published,
  "Non-Asian",            6584.57,          0.021,
  "Non-Asian",            21683.3,          0.045,
  "Japanese",             6584.57,          0.065,
  "Japanese",             21683.3,          0.127,
  "Asian (non-Japanese)", 6584.57,          0.012,
  "Asian (non-Japanese)", 21683.3,          0.025
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    RACE_JAPANESE = as.integer(race_group == "Japanese"),
    RACE_ASIAN    = as.integer(race_group == "Asian (non-Japanese)")
  )
fig2c$packaged <- solve_er(mod_ild_osi, "prob_ild", fig2c)

fig2c |>
  dplyr::select(race_group, AUC_OSIMERTINIB, published, packaged) |>
  dplyr::mutate(packaged = round(packaged, 4)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Race group" = race_group, "AUCss (nM*h)" = AUC_OSIMERTINIB,
    "Figure 2C (read off)" = published, "Packaged model" = packaged
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

stopifnot(
  # The figure is read to about +/- 0.003; a wrong scale or unit misses by
  # far more than that.
  all(abs(fig2c$packaged - fig2c$published) < 0.006)
)
```

```{r plot-figure-2c, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 2C of Johnson 2024: predicted ILD probability against osimertinib AUCss by race group (final model). Dashed lines mark the quartile boundaries printed on the published axis."}
grid_2c <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  AUC_OSIMERTINIB = exp(seq(log(5000), log(30000), length.out = 60)),
  race_group = c("Non-Asian", "Japanese", "Asian (non-Japanese)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    RACE_JAPANESE = as.integer(race_group == "Japanese"),
    RACE_ASIAN    = as.integer(race_group == "Asian (non-Japanese)")
  )
grid_2c$p <- solve_er(mod_ild_osi, "prob_ild", grid_2c)

ggplot(grid_2c, aes(AUC_OSIMERTINIB, p, linetype = race_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = auc_axis, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Osimertinib AUCss (nM*h)", y = "Probability of an ILD event",
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Check 2 -- the published placebo extrapolation

Johnson 2024 quotes the ILD probability of a placebo patient ("AUCss = 0") as
0.009% from the osimertinib model and 0.06% from the AZ5104 model,
"calculated from the intercept estimates in Table 1 and Table S7". Because the
exposure enters as `log(AUCss)`, a literal zero exposure gives a probability of
exactly 0; the quoted values are the probabilities at `log(AUCss) = 0`, i.e.
`expit(intercept)` for a non-Asian patient. The packaged intercepts reproduce
both numbers.

```{r check-placebo}
p_int <- c(
  osimertinib = solve_er(mod_ild_osi, "prob_ild",
                         data.frame(AUC_OSIMERTINIB = 1, RACE_JAPANESE = 0, RACE_ASIAN = 0)),
  az5104      = solve_er(mod_ild_az, "prob_ild",
                         data.frame(AUC_AZ5104 = 1, RACE_JAPANESE = 0, RACE_ASIAN = 0))
)
round(100 * p_int, 4)

stopifnot(
  round(100 * p_int[["osimertinib"]], 3) == 0.009,
  round(100 * p_int[["az5104"]], 2) == 0.06
)
```

# Virtual cohort

The cohort has 200 virtual patients in each of the three race groups of the
ILD model (non-Asian, Japanese, Asian non-Japanese). Each patient is
evaluated at 40, 80 and 160 mg once daily -- the doses of Figures 2D and 3B --
so the dose comparisons are paired. Body weight and baseline albumin follow
the truncated log-normal distributions used in the `Johnson_2025_osimertinib`
vignette (medians 61 kg and 39 g/L). Within the non-Asian group the White to
other split, and within the Asian non-Japanese group the Chinese to other-Asian
split, follow Table S3 (first-line plus second-or-later-line columns); the PK
model needs these finer groups for the AZ5104 clearance. Baseline LVEF is not
reported by Johnson 2024; it is drawn from a normal distribution with mean 63%
and SD 6%, restricted to 50-80% (an assumption, see below).

The between-patient random effects of the PK model are drawn in base R and
passed to `rxSolve()` as parameters, so the cohort does not depend on the
random-number stream of the installed rxode2.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20241101)
n_per_group <- 200
race_groups <- c("Non-Asian", "Japanese", "Asian (non-Japanese)")

sample_truncated_lognorm <- function(n, lo, hi, median_val, sd_log) {
  out <- numeric(0)
  while (length(out) < n) {
    draw <- exp(rnorm(n, mean = log(median_val), sd = sd_log))
    out <- c(out, draw[draw >= lo & draw <= hi])
  }
  out[seq_len(n)]
}

group <- rep(race_groups, each = n_per_group)
n_sub <- length(group)
u <- runif(n_sub)
# Table S3 (first-line + second-or-later-line): White 375 vs other non-Asian
# 135; Chinese 277 vs Asian non-Chinese non-Japanese 323.
pk_race <- dplyr::case_when(
  group == "Non-Asian" & u < 375 / 510 ~ "White",
  group == "Non-Asian" ~ "Other",
  group == "Japanese" ~ "Japanese",
  u < 277 / 600 ~ "Chinese",
  TRUE ~ "Asian_oth"
)

cohort <- tibble::tibble(
  id = seq_len(n_sub),
  race_group = group,
  WT  = sample_truncated_lognorm(n_sub, lo = 29, hi = 122, median_val = 61, sd_log = 0.21),
  ALB = sample_truncated_lognorm(n_sub, lo = 17, hi = 53.3, median_val = 39, sd_log = 0.13),
  RACE_CHINESE   = as.integer(pk_race == "Chinese"),
  RACE_JAPANESE  = as.integer(pk_race == "Japanese"),
  RACE_ASIAN_OTH = as.integer(pk_race == "Asian_oth"),
  RACE_OTHER     = as.integer(pk_race == "Other"),
  LVEF_BL = pmin(pmax(rnorm(n_sub, mean = 63, sd = 6), 50), 80)
)

omega <- rxode2::rxode2(mod_pk)$omega
eta <- matrix(rnorm(n_sub * nrow(omega)), n_sub) %*% chol(omega)
colnames(eta) <- rownames(omega)

# One observation record per patient is enough: the individual apparent
# clearances are time-invariant.
pk_events <- cohort |>
  dplyr::transmute(id, time = 0, amt = 0, evid = 0L, dvid = 1L,
                   WT, ALB, RACE_CHINESE, RACE_JAPANESE, RACE_ASIAN_OTH, RACE_OTHER)
pk_par <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_pk), events = pk_events,
                          params = data.frame(id = cohort$id, eta),
                          returnType = "data.frame")
cohort <- cohort |>
  dplyr::mutate(cl = pk_par$cl, cl_az5104 = pk_par$cl_az5104)

exposure <- tidyr::expand_grid(cohort, dose = c(40, 80, 160)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    AUC_OSIMERTINIB = dose / cl * 1e6 / mw_osimertinib,
    AUC_AZ5104      = fm_az5104 * dose / cl_az5104 * 1e6 / mw_osimertinib,
    RACE_JAPANESE   = as.integer(race_group == "Japanese"),
    RACE_ASIAN      = as.integer(race_group == "Asian (non-Japanese)")
  )
```

The simulated osimertinib AUCss by dose sits where the box plots of Figure 2A
put it (medians near 5500, 11 000 and 22 000 nM*h), and the random effects
carry the CL/F variability of the PK model (44.9% CV).

```{r check-exposure}
exposure |>
  dplyr::group_by(dose) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `Median osimertinib AUCss (nM*h)` = round(median(AUC_OSIMERTINIB)),
    `5th percentile` = round(quantile(AUC_OSIMERTINIB, 0.05)),
    `95th percentile` = round(quantile(AUC_OSIMERTINIB, 0.95)),
    `Median AZ5104 AUCss (nM*h)` = round(median(AUC_AZ5104)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename("Dose (mg QD)" = dose) |>
  knitr::kable()

typical_auc_80 <- 80 / exp(rxode2::rxode2(mod_pk)$theta[["lcl"]]) * 1e6 / mw_osimertinib
sd_log_cl <- sd(log(cohort$cl))
c(typical_auc_80 = typical_auc_80, sd_log_cl = sd_log_cl)

stopifnot(
  # The cohort median is near the typical-patient value; covariates move it
  # by a few percent only.
  abs(median(exposure$AUC_OSIMERTINIB[exposure$dose == 80]) / typical_auc_80 - 1) < 0.1,
  # The random effects were applied (omega of CL/F = 0.43 on the log scale);
  # covariates add a little on top.
  sd_log_cl > 0.35, sd_log_cl < 0.6
)
```

# Replicate Figure 2D -- ILD probability by dose and race

Johnson 2024 Figure 2D shows the predicted mean ILD probability at 40, 80 and
160 mg in each race group and in the overall population. The overall value
here weights the three groups by their share of the first-line plus
second-or-later-line population of Table S3 (non-Asian 510, Japanese 254,
Asian non-Japanese 600 of 1364).

```{r figure-2d}
exposure$p_ild_osi <- solve_er(mod_ild_osi, "prob_ild", exposure)
exposure$p_ild_az  <- solve_er(mod_ild_az, "prob_ild", exposure)

group_weight <- c("Non-Asian" = 510, "Japanese" = 254, "Asian (non-Japanese)" = 600) / 1364

by_group <- exposure |>
  dplyr::group_by(race_group, dose) |>
  dplyr::summarise(p_osi = mean(p_ild_osi), p_az = mean(p_ild_az), .groups = "drop")
overall <- by_group |>
  dplyr::mutate(w = group_weight[race_group]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(dose) |>
  dplyr::summarise(p_osi = sum(w * p_osi), p_az = sum(w * p_az), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(race_group = "Overall population")

# Grey predicted means read off Figure 2D.
fig2d <- tibble::tribble(
  ~race_group,            ~dose, ~published,
  "Non-Asian",            40,    0.020,
  "Non-Asian",            80,    0.032,
  "Non-Asian",            160,   0.047,
  "Japanese",             40,    0.067,
  "Japanese",             80,    0.095,
  "Japanese",             160,   0.142,
  "Asian (non-Japanese)", 40,    0.012,
  "Asian (non-Japanese)", 80,    0.020,
  "Asian (non-Japanese)", 160,   0.028,
  "Overall population",   40,    0.025,
  "Overall population",   80,    0.038,
  "Overall population",   160,   0.057
)

cmp_2d <- dplyr::bind_rows(by_group, overall) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(fig2d, by = c("race_group", "dose"))

cmp_2d |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(p_osi, p_az), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  dplyr::select(race_group, dose, published, p_osi, p_az) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Race group" = race_group, "Dose (mg QD)" = dose,
    "Figure 2D (read off)" = published,
    "Simulated, osimertinib model" = p_osi, "Simulated, AZ5104 model" = p_az
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

stopifnot(
  # Within 20% of the published means in every cell. The largest gap is the
  # Japanese group, which the cohort gives the overall weight distribution;
  # Johnson 2024 notes Japanese patients were lighter and had higher AUCss.
  all(abs(log(cmp_2d$p_osi / cmp_2d$published)) < log(1.2)),
  # The two exposure drivers describe the same events and agree closely.
  all(abs(log(cmp_2d$p_az / cmp_2d$p_osi)) < log(1.15))
)
```

```{r plot-figure-2d, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 2D of Johnson 2024: predicted mean ILD probability by dose and race group (bars: simulated, osimertinib-driven model; points: values read off the published figure)."}
cmp_2d |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(dose), p_osi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(y = published), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~race_group, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Osimertinib dose (mg once daily)", y = "Probability of an ILD event") +
  theme_bw()
```

At 80 mg the observed proportions in Figure 2D (about 2.8% non-Asian, 10.4%
Japanese, 2.2% Asian non-Japanese, 4.1% overall) sit on top of the
predictions, as the paper reports.

# Replicate Figure 3B -- LVEF-decrease probability by dose

The LVEF models need a baseline LVEF, which Johnson 2024 does not tabulate, so
the absolute probabilities below depend on the assumed baseline distribution.
The dose RATIO does not: in the logistic model a doubling of AUCss multiplies
the odds by `2^slope` whatever the baseline, which gives a check that is free
of that assumption.

```{r figure-3b}
exposure$p_lvef_osi <- solve_er(mod_lvef_osi, "prob_lvef_decrease", exposure)
exposure$p_lvef_az  <- solve_er(mod_lvef_az, "prob_lvef_decrease", exposure)

lvef_dose <- exposure |>
  dplyr::mutate(w = group_weight[race_group] / n_per_group) |>
  dplyr::group_by(dose) |>
  dplyr::summarise(p_osi = sum(w * p_lvef_osi), p_az = sum(w * p_lvef_az), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(published = c(0.024, 0.043, 0.076)) # Figure 3B model predictions, read off

lvef_dose |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(p_osi, p_az), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  dplyr::select(dose, published, p_osi, p_az) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (mg QD)" = dose, "Figure 3B (read off)" = published,
    "Simulated, osimertinib model" = p_osi, "Simulated, AZ5104 model" = p_az
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

# Odds ratio per doubling of dose, typical patient (exact) and published
# figure (from the read-off means).
odds <- function(p) p / (1 - p)
or_doubling <- c(
  model_exact = 2^0.921,
  figure_40_to_80 = odds(0.043) / odds(0.024),
  figure_80_to_160 = odds(0.076) / odds(0.043)
)
round(or_doubling, 2)

stopifnot(
  # Baseline-free check: the published dose steps imply the model's
  # odds ratio per doubling of exposure.
  all(abs(log(or_doubling[-1] / or_doubling[["model_exact"]])) < log(1.15)),
  # Assumption-dependent check (baseline LVEF not reported): same order of
  # magnitude as Figure 3B at every dose.
  all(abs(log(lvef_dose$p_osi / lvef_dose$published)) < log(1.3)),
  all(diff(lvef_dose$p_osi) > 0)
)
```

The observed rate at 80 mg (35/909 = 3.9%) lies inside the predicted
interval, while the comparator arms had 1/94 (chemotherapy) and 4/256
(comparator EGFR-TKI) events. Johnson 2024 notes that the 95% intervals at
80 mg and for the comparators largely overlap, so the exposure dependence of
LVEF events is uncertain and confounded by the small number of events and the
baseline LVEF.

# PKNCA

Not applicable: these are static landmark exposure-response models with no
time dimension and no concentration profile. Exposure enters as an AUCss
column; the steady-state AUCs of the companion PK model are validated with
PKNCA in the `Johnson_2025_osimertinib` vignette. The exposure check above
confirms that the dose / CL/F derivation used here lands on the published
AUCss distribution.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Exposure scale.** Johnson 2024 states "log-transformed" AUCss for the LVEF
  models only and never gives the exposure unit. The natural log of AUCss in
  nM*h is used for all four models; Check 1 shows it reproduces Figure 2C,
  and Check 2 reproduces the quoted placebo probabilities.
* **Zero exposure.** With `log(AUCss)` a placebo patient (AUCss = 0) has a
  predicted probability of exactly 0. The paper's quoted 0.009% / 0.06% are
  the probabilities at `log(AUCss) = 0`. The paper itself notes that the
  model, fitted to osimertinib-treated patients only, underestimates the
  background ILD rate.
* **Race encoding.** The ILD models' "Asian (non-Japanese)" covariate is
  encoded as `RACE_ASIAN` and is mutually exclusive with `RACE_JAPANESE`: a
  Japanese patient has `RACE_ASIAN = 0`. This differs from the companion PK
  model, where `RACE_ASIAN_OTH` excludes Chinese patients too.
* **AZ5104 AUCss.** Johnson 2024 does not print the formula for the AZ5104
  AUCss. It is taken as the molar steady-state value `fm * dose / (CLm/F)_i`
  of the PK model, with the fixed fm = 0.25. The supplementary NONMEM code
  scales the metabolite compartment by the AZ5104 molecular weight without
  a molar conversion, a 2.8% difference in AUCss that moves the logit by less
  than 0.02.
* **Placeholder residual.** The source fits a Bernoulli likelihood with Firth
  penalization and no random effects. Each model declares its probability as
  the observation with a fixed additive residual of 0.001 only so that rxode2
  accepts the model; it has no source counterpart.
* **Virtual cohort.** Body weight and albumin follow overall distributions for
  all race groups; Johnson 2024 notes Japanese patients were lighter, with
  higher AUCss, which is why the simulated Japanese means fall slightly below
  Figure 2D. Baseline LVEF (mean 63%, SD 6%, restricted to 50-80%) is an
  assumption, as the paper does not report it.
